[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **R warm-up.** Rebuild the Lecture 1 model, the regression
of the agreed valuation on the claimed valuation (both in \$ millions) for
the 874 deals for a share of the company. Make its residual-versus-fitted
plot: the fitted values on the horizontal axis and the
residuals on the vertical axis. Bring the plot to class:

```{r}
#| label: i02-prep-warmup

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your preparation

1. A curve in the residuals, for example below zero at both ends and above
   zero in the middle, challenges linearity. A spread that grows or shrinks
   from left to right, like a funnel, challenges constant variance.
2. An outlier has an unusually large residual: its outcome lies far from
   the fitted line. An influential observation changes the fitted line
   noticeably when you remove it. An outlier is not always influential,
   and an influential observation does not always have a large residual.
3. At small fitted values the residuals stay close to zero. At large fitted
   values they spread over several million dollars, like a funnel. The
   lecture material explains what this pattern means.
:::

## Lecture material

This section states what the regression model assumes and what each
assumption is needed for. It then goes through the assumptions one at a
time. For three of them you learn to read a plot of the residuals, and for
the other two you learn which questions about the data to ask instead. The
last part looks at single deals that move the line, and at how to check how
much the results depend on them.

### Start with a founder's question

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Lecture 1 gave you a number: each extra dollar of claimed valuation goes
with about 65 cents more agreed valuation, on average. Before you plan a negotiation around this number, ask whether you
can trust the line behind it. R draws a line through any data, also through
data that a straight line describes badly, and it gives no warning.

In [QM Basic Lecture 1](../basic/b01-introduction-data-analysis.qmd) you saw
that a few very large offers pull the mean up, while the median stays put. A
fitted line is a line of averages, so a few very large deals can pull it in
the same way. This lecture first lists what the model assumes. It then
checks each assumption in turn, mostly with plots of the residuals, and ends
with a search for the few deals that move the line most. Lecture 3 then
builds on this check when it measures how precise the slope is.

### The residual plot from the warm-up

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The code below is the warm-up code. It rebuilds the data and the model of
Lecture 1: the valuation agreed on air (`agreed_m`) regressed on the
valuation claimed by the founder (`claimed_m`), both in \$ millions, for the
874 Shark Tank deals for a share of the company. It only builds objects
and prints nothing. The figure below then plots the residuals of this model
against its fitted values.

```{r}
#| label: i02-build-model
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0)
vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6
vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6
val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-i02-warmup-residuals
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-cap: "Residuals against fitted values for the Lecture 1 valuation model, both in $ millions. On the left the residuals lie close to zero. On the right they spread over several million dollars."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of residuals against fitted agreed valuations, both in $ millions, with a dashed line at residual zero. Most points sit at fitted values below 5 million and stay within about 1 million of zero. Towards larger fitted values the points spread out, from about minus 8 to plus 13 million."
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0)
vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6
vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6
val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals)
resid_df <- data.frame(
  fitted = fitted(val_model),
  residual = residuals(val_model)
)

ggplot(resid_df, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#C98B2E",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6, colour = "#009E73") +
  annotate("text", x = 31.5, y = 0.9, label = "residual = 0",
           hjust = 1, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  labs(x = "Fitted agreed valuation ($ millions)",
       y = "Residual ($ millions)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )
```

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Residual plot** (residual-versus-fitted plot). A scatterplot with the
fitted values $\widehat Y_i$ on the horizontal axis and the residuals $e_i$
on the vertical axis. It shows how the residuals change from the left to
the right of the plot.
:::

In @fig-i02-warmup-residuals, both axes are in the units of the outcome,
\$1 million. A point above zero is a deal that was agreed at a higher valuation
than its fitted value. A point below zero is a deal that was agreed at a lower valuation than its
fitted value. To
read patterns in this plot, you first need to know what the model assumes.

### What each assumption supports

The model of Lecture 1 is

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i.
$$

Least squares gives a line for any data. Whether the numbers that come with
the line are reliable depends on a few assumptions. A founder who plans
with the 65 cents wants to know two things. Is the number right on average?
And how far from the truth could it be? The two answers need different
assumptions, so it helps to know which assumption supports which answer.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Model assumptions.** Conditions on the data and on the error terms
$\varepsilon_i$ under which the estimates, standard errors, tests, and
intervals of least squares are reliable.
:::

The assumptions are about the error terms $\varepsilon_i$ of the model. We
do not have the error terms in the data, because they depend on the
population line. The plots in this lecture therefore use the residuals
$e_i$, which are our estimates of the error terms (Lecture 1). The table
lists each assumption and says what goes wrong if it fails. Its third column
says how to check the assumption and what the check looks like when the
assumption holds and when it fails. The first three rows can be checked with
plots of the residuals. The last two follow from how the data were collected
and produced.

| Assumption | What it says in plain words | How to check it | What goes wrong if it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linearity | The average of $Y$ at each value of $X$ lies on a straight line: $E[Y\mid X=x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x$ | Residual plot. Holds: the residuals scatter around zero in every part of the range of fitted values. Fails: the residuals follow a curve, for example below zero at both ends and above zero in the middle | One slope misses part of the pattern, and the line is wrong in some parts of the range |
| Homoskedasticity (constant variance) | The errors have the same variance at every value of $X$: $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid X_i)=\sigma^2$ | Residual plot. Holds: the vertical spread of the residuals is about the same from left to right, an even band. Fails: the vertical spread grows or shrinks along the fitted values, like a funnel | The slope stays unbiased, but the usual standard errors, tests, and intervals are wrong |
| Normality of the errors | At each value of $X$, the errors follow a normal distribution | Normal Q-Q plot of the standardised residuals. Holds: the points lie close to the straight reference line. Fails: the points bend away from the line, usually at one or both ends | In small samples the t and F distributions of Lecture 3 are no longer exact. In large samples this matters little |
| Independence (random sampling) | The observations are drawn independently: the error of one row says nothing about the error of another row | No plot. Check how the data were collected. Holds: each row was drawn separately, for example customers drawn at random from a long list. Fails: rows share something that affects the outcome, such as the same shop, week, or episode | The usual standard errors are often too small, so intervals are too narrow. A sample that is not random can also bias the line |
| Zero conditional mean (exogeneity): no omitted confounder | The error averages zero at every value of $X$: $E[\varepsilon_i\mid X_i]=0$. For a causal reading: no other cause of $Y$ that is missing from the model is related to $X$ | No plot. Check how the values of $X$ came about. Holds: $X$ is unrelated to other causes of $Y$, for example because $X$ was set at random. Fails: another cause of $Y$ that is missing from the model is related to $X$ | The slope is not the effect of changing $X$. It still describes how average outcomes differ across values of $X$ |

The rows support different conclusions. Linearity, independent
observations, and zero conditional mean together make the estimated slope
$\hat\beta_1$ unbiased: across many samples, it is correct on average.
Homoskedasticity and independence are needed for the usual standard errors,
and so for the t-tests and intervals of Lecture 3. Normality of the errors
makes these tests and intervals exact in small samples. In large samples
they hold approximately without it, because of the central limit theorem.

No row of the table says that the data are normal. This answers the prediction
question from before class: the outcome does not need to be normally
distributed, and neither does the predictor. The agreed valuations are
strongly right-skewed, and this skew alone does not break any assumption.
The assumptions are about the average of $Y$ at each $X$, about the errors,
and about how the data were produced. They are not about the histogram of $Y$ or the histogram of
$X$.

### Checking the assumptions one at a time

The table gives a short version of each check. This section goes through
the five assumptions in the order of the table. For each of the first three
you first see a clear invented example in which the assumption holds and
one in which it fails. You then read the same kind of plot for the Shark
Tank model. For independence and zero conditional mean you see why the
residuals cannot show them, and which questions about the data you ask
instead.

#### Linearity

Linearity does not say that individual outcomes lie on a line. It says that
the average outcome at each value of the predictor follows a line. Think of
a founder who regresses weekly orders on weekly advertising spending. If
each extra €100 of advertising brings about the same number of extra orders
at low and at high spending, the average follows a line. If extra
advertising brings fewer and fewer extra orders, the average follows a curve
that flattens out, and one straight line cannot describe it.
@fig-i02-linearity shows both situations with invented data for 60 weeks. We
chose the true average in each column, so we know whether linearity holds.

```{r}
#| label: fig-i02-linearity
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Invented weekly orders and advertising spending for 60 weeks. Left column: the average number of orders rises by the same amount for every extra €100, so linearity holds. Right column: the gain from advertising flattens out, so linearity fails. Top row: orders against advertising with the fitted straight line. Bottom row: the residuals of that line against its fitted values, with the gold dashed line at residual zero."
#| fig-alt: "Four panels. Top left: points scattered evenly around a rising straight line. Top right: points that rise steeply and then flatten, with a straight line that lies above the points at both ends and below them in the middle. Bottom left: residuals in an even band around zero with no curve. Bottom right: residuals below zero at the left and right ends and above zero in the middle, an arch."
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(802)
n_w <- 60
ad <- runif(n_w, 0, 10)                               # advertising, in €100
orders_lin <- 40 + 3 * ad + rnorm(n_w, 0, 3)          # straight-line average
orders_cur <- 40 + 14 * log1p(ad) + rnorm(n_w, 0, 1.5)  # average flattens
m_lin <- lm(orders_lin ~ ad)
m_cur <- lm(orders_cur ~ ad)

col_names <- c("Linearity holds", "Linearity fails")
data_df <- data.frame(
  case = factor(rep(col_names, each = n_w), levels = col_names),
  x = c(ad, ad), y = c(orders_lin, orders_cur),
  fit = c(fitted(m_lin), fitted(m_cur)),
  res = c(residuals(m_lin), residuals(m_cur))
)
plot_df <- data.frame(
  case = rep(data_df$case, 2),
  row = rep(c("Orders against advertising",
              "Residuals against fitted values"), each = 2 * n_w),
  x = c(data_df$x, data_df$fit),
  y = c(data_df$y, data_df$res),
  line = c(data_df$fit, rep(NA, 2 * n_w))
)
plot_df$panel <- factor(
  paste(plot_df$case, ifelse(plot_df$row == "Orders against advertising",
                             "(data and line)", "(residuals)")),
  levels = c("Linearity holds (data and line)", "Linearity fails (data and line)",
             "Linearity holds (residuals)", "Linearity fails (residuals)"))
zero_df <- data.frame(
  panel = factor(c("Linearity holds (residuals)", "Linearity fails (residuals)"),
                 levels = levels(plot_df$panel)),
  yintercept = 0
)

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_hline(data = zero_df, aes(yintercept = yintercept),
             colour = "#C98B2E", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = subset(plot_df, !is.na(line)), aes(y = line),
            colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.8, colour = "#009E73") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Advertising in €100 (top) or fitted orders (bottom)",
       y = "Orders (top) or residual (bottom)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )
```

Read the figure column by column. In the left column the orders scatter
evenly around the straight line. Its residuals form a band around zero, with
points above and below zero in every part of the plot. This is what a
residual plot looks like when linearity holds. In the right column the gain
from advertising flattens out at high spending. The straight line lies above
the data at low and at high spending, and below the data in between. So the
residuals are negative at both ends and positive in the middle, an arch. A
curve like this in a residual plot, an arch or a U, shows that linearity
fails. Here one constant slope understates the gain from advertising at low
spending and overstates it at high spending. Lecture 6 shows how a curved
term in the model captures such a pattern.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Now read @fig-i02-warmup-residuals for
linearity. Ignore the spread for a moment and look at where the middle of
the cloud lies. In every part of the range there are residuals above and
below zero, and the cloud shows no arch or U. A short calculation makes this
reading precise. The code sorts the deals by the claimed valuation into five
groups, each with about a fifth of the deals. It then prints the average
residual in each group:

```{r}
#| label: i02-mean-by-fifth
fifth <- cut(vals$claimed_m,
             breaks = quantile(vals$claimed_m, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2)),
             include.lowest = TRUE)
round(tapply(residuals(val_model), fifth, mean), 2)   # average residual
```

The labels above the numbers are the ranges of claimed valuations, in
\$ millions. The groups hold between 146 and 206 deals, not exactly 175,
because many founders claim the same round amounts, such as \$1 million. The
output gives the average residuals, also in \$ millions: 0.10, 0.06,
0.12, $-0.26$, and $-0.08$. They do not form an arch or a U, and they are
small next to the misses for single deals, which reach several million
dollars. So the plot agrees with linearity.

#### Homoskedasticity (constant variance)

Homoskedasticity is about the vertical spread of the errors. It says that
the errors scatter equally widely at every value of the predictor. It does
not say that all residuals have the same size. When the spread changes with
the predictor, this is called **heteroskedasticity**. Business data often
show it. Take shops of different sizes. The monthly revenue of a small shop
may differ from its fitted value by a few thousand euros, and that of a
large shop by tens of thousands. @fig-i02-spread shows both situations with
invented data for 90 shops, with monthly revenue regressed on floor space.

```{r}
#| label: fig-i02-spread
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Residuals against fitted values for two invented regressions of the monthly revenue of 90 shops on their floor space. Left: the vertical spread is the same everywhere, so homoskedasticity holds. Right: the vertical spread grows along the fitted values, like a funnel, so homoskedasticity fails. The gold dashed line marks residual zero."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of residuals against fitted revenue in thousands of euros. Left: an even horizontal band of points around zero, equally wide from left to right. Right: a band that is narrow at small fitted values and wide at large fitted values, like a funnel lying on its side."
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(803)
n_s <- 90
space <- runif(n_s, 20, 500)                         # floor space, in m2
rev_const <- 10 + 0.12 * space + rnorm(n_s, 0, 8)    # same spread everywhere
rev_funnel <- 10 + 0.12 * space +
  rnorm(n_s, 0, 0.04 * space)                        # spread grows with size
m_const <- lm(rev_const ~ space)
m_funnel <- lm(rev_funnel ~ space)

case_names <- c("Homoskedasticity holds", "Homoskedasticity fails")
spread_df <- data.frame(
  case = factor(rep(case_names, each = n_s), levels = case_names),
  fitted = c(fitted(m_const), fitted(m_funnel)),
  residual = c(residuals(m_const), residuals(m_funnel))
)

ggplot(spread_df, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#C98B2E",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.8, colour = "#009E73") +
  facet_wrap(~ case) +
  labs(x = "Fitted monthly revenue (€1,000)",
       y = "Residual (€1,000)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )
```

In the left panel the residuals form an even horizontal band: the vertical
spread is about the same at small and at large fitted values. This is what
a residual plot looks like when homoskedasticity holds. In the right panel
the band is narrow on the left and wide on the right, like a funnel lying on
its side. The vertical spread of the residuals grows along the fitted
values, so homoskedasticity fails. A band that narrows from left to right
is heteroskedasticity too. Both panels have the same average pattern, so
the problem is not the line itself but how far the shops scatter around it.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Now look for heteroskedasticity in
@fig-i02-warmup-residuals. At small fitted values the residuals stay close
to the zero line. At larger fitted values they spread over several million
dollars. The same five groups as in the linearity check confirm what the
plot shows. The code gives the standard deviation of the residuals in each
group:

```{r}
#| label: i02-spread-by-fifth
round(tapply(residuals(val_model), fifth, sd), 2)   # spread of the residuals
round(tapply(vals$agreed_m, fifth, mean), 2)         # average agreed valuation
```

The first output gives the standard deviations of the residuals, in
\$ millions. They are \$0.14 million in the fifth with the smallest
claims, then \$0.36, \$1.19, and \$1.08 million, and \$3.61 million in the
fifth with the largest claims. The last is about 25 times the first. So the
spread broadly grows with the size of the claim, like a funnel. The second
output shows that the deals also get larger: the average agreed valuation
rises from \$0.28 million in the first fifth to \$7.83 million in the last. Relative to the size of the deals the
spread is more stable: in every fifth the standard deviation lies between
0.46 and 0.89 times the average agreed valuation of that fifth. This makes
economic sense: founders and sharks can disagree by much more money about a
\$20 million company than about a \$200,000 company. This pattern is
heteroskedasticity. The usual standard errors assume one common variance
$\sigma^2$, so here they depend on an assumption that probably does not
hold. The slope itself stays unbiased, because heteroskedasticity is not
part of the conditions for an unbiased slope. Lecture 3 returns to this
point.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Try it: annotate a residual plot

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Use a printed copy or a sketch of
@fig-i02-warmup-residuals.

*Step 1 (given).* The horizontal dashed line marks residual zero. Points
above it are deals with an agreed valuation above the fitted value. Points
below it are deals with an agreed valuation below the fitted value.

*Step 2 (you).* Draw two rough curves around the residuals, one along
the top of the points and one along the bottom, from the left edge to the
right edge of the plot. Does the band between the two curves stay equally
wide?

*Step 3 (you).* Name the assumption that your two curves challenge. Then
write one sentence that says whether the average of the residuals also
moves away from zero in some part of the plot.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

The band between the two curves widens strongly from left to right. Deals
with small fitted valuations lie within a few hundred thousand dollars of the
line. Deals with large fitted valuations lie within several million. The
vertical spread grows along the fitted values like a funnel, which shows
heteroskedasticity, so it challenges homoskedasticity. The average residual
stays near zero across the range, so the plot does not show a clear
violation of linearity. You read the same plot twice, once for each
assumption.
:::
:::

#### Normality of the errors

The third row of the table is normality of the errors. It matters most when
you have few observations, for example a young venture with 20 weeks of
sales data. The tests and intervals of Lecture 3 then rely on it. A
histogram of the residuals gives a first impression, but it is hard to judge
the ends of a distribution from a histogram. A **normal Q-Q plot**
(quantile-quantile plot) shows the ends more clearly. It puts the
standardised residuals in order and compares them with the values that a
normal distribution would give. A standardised residual is a residual
measured in standard deviations, and the section on outliers below defines
it precisely. The horizontal axis shows where a residual of this rank would
lie if the errors were normal. The vertical axis shows where the residual
actually lies. If the residuals are close to normal, the points lie along
the reference line.

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} @fig-i02-qq compares an invented case with
normal errors and the Shark Tank model. The invented case has the same
number of observations, 874, so that the two panels are easy to compare.

```{r}
#| label: fig-i02-qq
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Normal Q-Q plots of standardised residuals. Left: an invented regression with 874 observations and normal errors, so normality holds. Right: the Shark Tank valuation model. Both ends leave the line, so normality fails: a few deals were agreed far above and far below their fitted valuation."
#| fig-alt: "Two normal Q-Q plots with theoretical quantiles from about minus 3 to plus 3 on the horizontal axis and standardised residuals on the vertical axis. Left: the points follow the rising reference line from end to end. Right: in the middle the points follow the line, but at the left end they fall below it, down to about minus 5, and at the right end they rise far above it, up to about 8."
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0)
vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6
vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6
val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals)

set.seed(805)
x_inv <- runif(874, 0, 10)
y_inv <- 1 + 0.6 * x_inv + rnorm(874, 0, 1)          # normal errors
m_inv <- lm(y_inv ~ x_inv)

qq_names <- c("Invented: normal errors", "Shark Tank valuation model")
qq_df <- data.frame(
  case = factor(rep(qq_names, each = 874), levels = qq_names),
  rs = c(rstandard(m_inv), rstandard(val_model))
)

ggplot(qq_df, aes(sample = rs)) +
  geom_qq_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_qq(colour = "#009E73", alpha = 0.4, size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ case) +
  labs(x = "Normal theoretical quantile",
       y = "Standardised residual") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )
```

In the left panel the points follow the reference line from one end to the
other. Small departures at the very ends are normal in any sample. This is
what a Q-Q plot looks like when normality holds. In the right panel the
middle of the distribution is close to the line, but both ends bend away
from it, the upper end more strongly. The Shark Tank residuals have more
extreme values on both sides than a normal distribution has. We say that
such a distribution has heavy tails. As a benchmark, under a normal
distribution about 3 in 1,000 values lie beyond $\pm 3$ standard
deviations, so about 2 or 3 of the 874 deals. Here 25 deals do, and the most
extreme standardised residual is about 8. So normality fails for this model.

Two base R commands draw the Shark Tank panel without the styling of the
figure:

```{r}
#| label: fig-i02-qq-base
#| fig-cap: "Normal Q-Q plot of the standardised residuals of the valuation model, drawn with base R."
#| fig-alt: "Base R version of the normal Q-Q plot of the standardised residuals of the valuation model, with the same shape: points on the reference line in the middle and far from it at both ends."
qqnorm(rstandard(val_model))
qqline(rstandard(val_model))
```

How much does this failure matter? Normal errors are needed for exact t and F
distributions in small samples. With 874 observations the tests and
intervals of Lecture 3 still hold approximately without normal errors,
because of the central limit theorem: averages over many observations are
close to normal, and the estimated slope is such an average. The
approximation is weaker when a few extreme deals decide where the line lies.
Very extreme outliers distort both the line and its standard errors, in
samples of any size. The section on outliers below therefore looks at these
deals one by one.

#### Independence

Independence says that the error of one row tells you nothing about the
error of another row. It is a property of how the data were collected, not
of the numbers themselves. It holds when the rows are drawn separately from
each other, as in a random sample of customers from a long customer list.
It fails when rows share something that affects the outcome. Three business
examples show how this happens.

- Weekly sales of one shop. A busy week, for example during a local event,
  is often followed by another busy week. The errors of neighbouring weeks
  then move together.
- Customers of the same shop. In a survey of customer satisfaction across
  20 shops, the customers of one shop meet the same staff in the same
  location. Their errors move together.
- Shark Tank episodes. Pitches in the same episode face the same panel of
  sharks on the same day, and the same few sharks appear in hundreds of
  deals. Their rows share negotiators, moods, and editing decisions.

When rows are related but you treat them as independent, the data seem to
contain more information than they really do. The 874 deals contain
somewhat less information than 874 unrelated deals would, and the usual
standard errors are too small. A residual-versus-fitted plot cannot show
this problem, because it does not show which rows belong together. Only
knowledge of how the data were collected tells you which rows might be
related. So before you trust the standard errors, ask: were the rows drawn
separately, or do some of them share a person, a firm, a place, or a time?

#### Zero conditional mean (exogeneity)

The last row of the table matters for how you read the slope. It uses two
new terms, defined together here.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Confounder.** A variable that is not in the model and that affects both
$X$ and $Y$.

**Omitted variable bias.** The distortion of the slope of $X$ that arises
when a confounder is left out of the model: the slope also picks up the
relationship between the confounder and $Y$.
:::

If you read the slope as a description of how average outcomes differ
across values of $X$, the error is just the distance from the line of
averages. Linearity then already makes the errors average zero at every
value of $X$. If you read the slope as the effect of changing $X$, the error
term contains all other causes of $Y$. Zero conditional mean then says that
these other causes are unrelated to $X$. An omitted confounder breaks this
assumption, and the slope is then too large or too small as a measure of
the effect of $X$. This is omitted variable bias.

No residual plot can show a confounder. Least squares always gives residuals
with a mean of zero and no straight-line relation to $X$, even when the
error terms are related to $X$. So the residual plot looks clean even when
a confounder exists. Instead, ask how the values of $X$ came about, and
which common causes of $X$ and $Y$ are plausible but missing from the data.
Three business examples show the kind of reasoning this takes.

- Price and demand. A café cuts its prices in weeks when demand is already
  weak. Weak demand lowers the number of orders and also leads to the price
  cut, so a regression of orders on price mixes the two.
- Advertising and season. A webshop advertises most in December, when
  people buy more anyway. The advertising slope then also picks up the
  December rush.
- Network ties on Shark Tank. Suppose founders with strong investor
  networks both claim higher valuations, because they know the market, and
  get better deals, because the sharks know them. Network strength is not
  recorded in the data, so it is an omitted confounder for a causal reading
  of the valuation slope.

In each example the slope still describes how average outcomes differ
across values of $X$, which is useful for comparison and prediction. To read
it as the effect of changing $X$, you need a design in which $X$ is
unrelated to the other causes. The A/B tests of Lecture 5 set $X$ at random
for exactly this reason. Lecture 4 shows omitted variable bias in an
example, and shows how adding a confounder to the model as a control
variable removes it.

### Analysing residuals: outliers and influential observations

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The residual plots showed that a few deals lie
far from the line. A founder with an ordinary company wants to know whether
the 65 cents describe the typical deal or rest mainly on a handful of very
large deals. You would not want one huge number to drive the slope. This
section first finds the unusual deals. It then checks how much the results
change without them, which is called a sensitivity analysis.

A first check needs no plot. The function `summary()` gives the smallest
residual, the largest residual, the mean, the median, and the two quartiles.
[Basic Lecture 1](../basic/b01-introduction-data-analysis.qmd#b01-quartiles)
defines the median and the quartiles: at least a quarter of the values lie
at or below the first quartile, half at or below the median, and at least
three quarters at or below the third quartile.

```{r}
#| label: i02-residual-line
summary(residuals(val_model))
```

::: {#exm-i02-residual-line}
## Worked example: reading the summary of the residuals

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Read the numbers one by one, all in \$ millions:

- The median residual is about $-0.01$: the typical deal lies almost
  exactly on the fitted line.
- The middle half of all residuals, from the first to the third quartile,
  runs from $-0.40$ to $0.17$: a band about \$570,000 wide.
- The minimum is about $-7.8$ and the maximum about $13.4$: one deal
  was agreed \$7.8 million below its fitted valuation and another \$13.4 million
  above. As a benchmark, the average agreed valuation is \$2.2 million, so
  each of these misses is several times the size of an average deal.

The mean is zero, as it always is when the model has an intercept. If no
deal were extreme, the largest residuals would be a few times the width of
the middle half. Here they are 14 to 24 times as large. A few deals miss the line
by far more than the typical deal does, and such deals can strongly change
the fitted line. The same numbers, without the mean, appear at the top of
`summary(val_model)`. Lecture 3 explains this output.
:::

Two standard tools make this check precise. A **standardised residual**,
`rstandard()`, is a residual divided by its standard deviation, so it
measures the residual in standard deviations. Values beyond about $\pm 3$ are large by any
common standard. **Cook's distance**, `cooks.distance()`, measures how much the
whole fitted line would move if one observation were removed. A common
threshold is $4/n$: you look more closely at observations above it.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Outlier.** An observation with an unusually large residual: its outcome
lies far from the fitted line. A common rule is a standardised residual
beyond $\pm 3$.

**Influential observation.** An observation that changes the fitted line
noticeably when it is removed. A common rule is a Cook's distance above
$4/n$.

**Sensitivity analysis.** Fitting the model again under a different, stated
choice, for example without the influential observations, and comparing
the results with the original fit.
:::

```{r}
#| label: i02-influence
rs <- rstandard(val_model)
cd <- cooks.distance(val_model)

sum(abs(rs) > 3)               # standardised residuals beyond 3
sum(cd > 4 / nobs(val_model))  # Cook's distance above 4/n
vals[order(cd, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3],
      c("claimed_m", "agreed_m")]
```

The code computes both measures for every deal. It then counts the deals
beyond each threshold and prints the claimed and agreed valuations of the
three deals with the largest Cook's distance. The command `nobs(val_model)`
gives the number of observations $n$ that the model uses, here 874.

Twenty-five deals have standardised residuals beyond $\pm 3$, and 64 have a
Cook's distance above $4/n$. These are 3% and 7% of the 874 deals. The most
influential deal claimed a valuation of \$50 million and was agreed at
\$25 million, half of the claim. The next two claimed \$45 million and
\$28 million and were agreed at \$36 million and \$28 million. For comparison, the median claim is \$2 million, and only 3% of
the deals claim \$20 million or more. Such deals lie far to the right of all
other deals. An observation like this has high leverage: like a long lever,
it can pull the fitted line towards itself. @fig-i02-influence marks the 64
deals in the scatterplot.

```{r}
#| label: fig-i02-influence
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-cap: "The 874 deals with the fitted line, full range shown. Orange points have a Cook's distance above 4/n. The labelled deal (claimed $50 million, agreed $25 million) moves the fitted line most: it sits far to the right (high leverage), so it pulls on the line like a lever."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of agreed against claimed valuation in $ millions, with the rising fitted line. Most grey points crowd at claims below 10 million. Orange flagged points include many deals with claims above 10 million and some smaller deals far from the line. A label marks the deal at claimed 50, agreed 25, far to the right and below the line."
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0)
vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6
vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6
val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals)
cd <- cooks.distance(val_model)
vals$flagged <- cd > 4 / nrow(vals)
top <- which.max(cd)

ggplot(vals, aes(x = claimed_m, y = agreed_m)) +
  geom_point(data = subset(vals, !flagged),
             colour = "grey75", alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(val_model)[1],
              slope = coef(val_model)[2],
              colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = subset(vals, flagged),
             colour = "#D55E00", size = 2.2) +
  annotate("text", x = vals$claimed_m[top] - 1.2, y = vals$agreed_m[top],
           label = "claimed 50, agreed 25",
           hjust = 1, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  labs(x = "Valuation claimed by the founder ($ millions)",
       y = "Valuation agreed on air ($ millions)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )
```

Do the flagged deals drive the founder's number? The sensitivity analysis
fits the same model twice more: once without the single most influential
deal, and once without all 64 flagged deals. The rule for the second fit is
the stated threshold, a Cook's distance above $4/n$, not a choice made after
looking at the slope. The code prints the intercept and the slope of each
fit.

```{r}
#| label: i02-fit-without-flagged
coef(lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals[-which.max(cd), ]))
coef(lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals[cd <= 4 / nobs(val_model), ]))
```

Without the deal claimed at \$50 million, the slope rises a little, from
0.649 to 0.666: about 67 cents instead of 65 cents per claimed dollar, a
change of 3%. Without all 64 flagged deals, the slope falls to 0.567: about
57 cents per claimed dollar, 13% less than with all deals. So no single deal
decides the slope, but the 7% of flagged deals together move it noticeably.
The intercepts stay close to zero in all three fits, between
$-\$0.12$ million and \$0.05 million. The flagged deals are real pitches, so
the fit without them does not replace the fit with all deals. It shows how
much the result depends on a few large deals, and a reader of your analysis
needs both numbers: 65 cents with all deals and 57 cents without the
flagged ones.

What should you do with a flagged observation? Follow three steps, in this
order:

1. **Investigate.** Is it a data error, or a real pitch? Here the valuations
   of the flagged deals match their recorded amounts and shares, so we treat
   these deals as real.
2. **Check and report.** Refit the model without the flagged observations,
   as in the sensitivity analysis above. Say which observations you flagged
   and with which rule, and report both fits if the results change.
3. **Decide openly.** Keep or drop an observation only for a stated reason:
   a data error, a rule that you fixed before looking at the results, or
   knowledge that the observation comes from a different situation. State
   the decision and the reason. Never drop rows silently or because they do
   not fit your story.

::: {.caveat-box}
<span class="label">What a residual check can and cannot show</span>

- A residual plot without a pattern agrees with linearity and
  homoskedasticity. An omitted confounder and dependent errors do not show
  up in a plot, so they need knowledge of how the data were produced.
- Heteroskedasticity or an influential deal is a finding to report. Report
  it, and check with a sensitivity analysis how much it changes the results.
- Keeping or dropping an unusual observation is a decision that you make from
  knowledge of the data or a stated rule, and that you state openly.

**What you can do with it:** before you trust a fitted line, look at its
residual plot and at the few points that move it most. If the conclusion changes
without them, say so.
:::

### Answering the driving question

Under what conditions should we trust the Lecture 1 line? The slope is
right on average if the average of $Y$ lies on a straight line, the deals
are independent, and no omitted confounder is related to the claim. The
usual standard errors also need a constant spread of the errors
(homoskedasticity) and independence. Normal errors matter only in small
samples.

What do its residuals reveal? The average residuals stay close to zero
across the range of claims, so the plots agree with linearity. But the
vertical spread grows with the size of the claim, from a standard deviation
of \$0.14 million in the fifth with the smallest claims to \$3.61 million in
the fifth with the largest. This heteroskedasticity does not bias the slope,
but it makes the usual standard errors doubtful. And 64 deals, 7% of all
deals, have a Cook's distance above $4/n$. Without them the slope falls
from 0.65 to 0.57. Independence and zero conditional mean cannot be seen in
any plot. They depend on how the show works, for example on shared episodes
and on founders' networks.

As a founder you might expect about 57 to 65 cents of agreed valuation per
extra dollar of claimed valuation, under the assumption that your company is
like the companies on the show. The 65 cents describe all deals, and the 57
cents describe the deals without the 64 that move the line most. Lecture 3 calculates
standard errors, intervals, and tests for this model. The spread that grows
with the claim and the influential deals limit how much you can trust those
results.

::: {.founder-box}
<span class="label">A founder's decision (invented example)</span>

You regress weekly orders on weekly advertising spending. One week in your
data includes a catering order of 200 meal boxes, in a week with high
advertising. With that week the advertising slope is 0.15 orders per euro.
Without that week it is 0.09. You earn 4 euros of margin per order. Which
slope do you use to plan next term's advertising budget?

Try it yourself first.

1. What do the two slopes say about 100 euros of advertising, in orders and
   in margin?
2. Why does one week change the slope so much?
3. Decide which slope to plan with, and what to report.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## See the solution

1. With the slope of 0.15: 15 more orders and 60 euros of margin. With
   0.09: 9 more orders and 36 euros of margin.
2. The catering week is an influential observation: an unusually large
   outcome at a high value of the predictor. It pulls the line up at high
   spending, so the slope gets steeper. One week out of many changes the
   slope by 40%, from 0.15 to 0.09.
3. Do not base the budget on a fit that depends on one single week.
   Catering is a different business from selling single meal boxes every
   day. Report both fits, plan the daily business with the slope of 0.09,
   and look at catering separately. Do not simply delete the week.
:::
:::

This lecture gave you a routine to follow before you rely on a fitted line:
check each assumption with a residual plot or with knowledge of the data,
and test with a sensitivity analysis how much a few unusual observations
move the result. For the Shark Tank deals, the line describes the average
pattern well, with about 57 to 65 cents of agreed valuation per claimed
dollar. One practical question is still open. The slope comes from one
sample of 874 deals, and another sample would give a somewhat different
number. Before planning a negotiation with it, a founder wants to know how
far the true slope could plausibly be from 65 cents, and how close the line
comes to the valuation of a single deal. Lecture 3 answers both questions:
it measures how precise the slope is and how much of the variation in agreed
valuations the line explains.

**Next:** Lecture 3 adds the standard error, the confidence interval, the
t-test, $R^2$, and the F-test to the fitted line.

:::

## After class

After the lecture, work through all the practice below.

### Read the lecture material

Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture
covered the main points. The text has every step, every example, and all the
code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still
unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly.

### Recall questions

1. Which assumption says that the average of $Y$ at each value of $X$ lies
   on a straight line?
2. Must the outcome variable be normally distributed? Why or why not?
3. What does it suggest when the vertical spread of the residuals grows
   along the fitted values, like a funnel?
4. Which assumptions can you not check with a residual plot alone?
5. What do a standardised residual and Cook's distance each measure?
6. What are the three steps for handling a flagged observation?
7. Which assumptions make the slope unbiased, and which assumptions do the
   usual standard errors need?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

1. Linearity, $E[Y\mid X=x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x$.
2. No. The assumptions are about the errors at each value of the predictor
   and about how the data were produced. They are not about the
   distribution of $Y$ or of $X$ on its own.
3. Heteroskedasticity: the variance of the errors is not constant.
4. Independence and zero conditional mean (no omitted confounder). They
   require knowledge of how the data were collected. A residual plot cannot
   show them, because least squares makes the residuals unrelated to $X$
   even when the error terms are related to it.
5. A standardised residual measures how unusual one observation's residual
   is, in standard-deviation units. Cook's distance measures how much
   the whole fitted line moves if that observation is removed.
6. Investigate, check and report with a sensitivity analysis, and decide
   openly with a stated reason.
7. Unbiased slope: linearity, independent observations, and zero
   conditional mean. Usual standard errors: homoskedasticity and
   independence. Normality of the errors is needed only for exact tests in
   small samples.
:::

### Finish a half-worked example: diagnose three residual plots

For each panel of @fig-i02-three-plots, write one sentence: which
assumption, if any, does the plot challenge?

Plot A (given). The residuals follow a U shape. The average residual is
negative in the middle and positive at the ends, so the plot challenges
linearity.

Plot B and Plot C (you). Write the sentence for each of them in the same
way.

```{r}
#| label: fig-i02-three-plots
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-cap: "Three simulated residual-versus-fitted plots. The gold dashed line marks residual zero in each panel."
#| fig-alt: "Three panels of residuals against fitted values from 1 to 9. Plot A: the residuals form a U shape, below zero in the middle and above zero at both ends. Plot B: the residuals form a band around zero that is narrow on the left and wide on the right. Plot C: the residuals form an even band around zero with no visible pattern."
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(1204)
n_p <- 120
f_p <- seq(1, 9, length.out = n_p)
res_a <- 1.6 * (f_p - 5)^2 / 8 - 1 + rnorm(n_p, 0, 0.55)
res_b <- rnorm(n_p, 0, 0.15 + 0.16 * f_p)
res_c <- rnorm(n_p, 0, 0.8)

plots_df <- data.frame(
  panel = rep(c("Plot A", "Plot B", "Plot C"), each = n_p),
  fitted = rep(f_p, 3),
  residual = c(res_a, res_b, res_c)
)
zero_lab <- data.frame(
  panel = c("Plot A", "Plot B", "Plot C"),
  x = 1,
  y = c(max(res_a), max(res_b), max(res_c))
)

ggplot(plots_df, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#C98B2E",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6, colour = "#009E73") +
  geom_text(data = zero_lab, aes(x = x, y = y, label = "residual = 0"),
            hjust = 0, colour = "#17324D", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Fitted value", y = "Residual") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

Plot B: the vertical spread of the residuals grows along the fitted value,
like a funnel. This shows heteroskedasticity, so it challenges
homoskedasticity. Plot C: no visible pattern. The plot agrees with
linearity and homoskedasticity, the two assumptions it can show.
Independence and zero conditional mean need knowledge of how the data were
produced.
:::

### Practice: diagnostics for your own model

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Regress the equity offered by the founder, in percent
(`equity_offered_pct`), on the season (`season`), using all 1,441 pitches.
Produce the residual-versus-fitted plot and the normal Q-Q plot. Interpret
each in one or two sentences. Then count the standardised residuals beyond $\pm 3$
and the observations with a Cook's distance above $4/n$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

```{r}
#| label: i02-practice-equity
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Residuals against fitted values (left) and normal Q-Q plot of the standardised residuals (right) for the regression of equity offered on season."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left: residuals of equity offered against fitted values, in sixteen vertical stripes between about 7 and 20 percent fitted equity, most residuals between about minus 10 and plus 15 points and a few up to about 83 points. Right: normal Q-Q plot whose points follow the line in the middle and bend sharply upwards at the right end."
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
equity_model <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks)
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.4, 1.3, 0.7), las = 1)
plot(fitted(equity_model), residuals(equity_model),
     pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#0072B2", alpha.f = 0.30),
     bty = "n", xlab = "Fitted equity offered (%)",
     ylab = "Residual (pp)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#D55E00")
qqnorm(rstandard(equity_model), pch = 16,
       col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#009E73", alpha.f = 0.35),
       bty = "n", main = "", xlab = "Normal theoretical quantile",
       ylab = "Standardised residual")
qqline(rstandard(equity_model), col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2)
par(old_par)
max(residuals(equity_model))
c(big_rstandard = sum(abs(rstandard(equity_model)) > 3),
  cooks_flagged = sum(cooks.distance(equity_model) > 4 / nobs(equity_model)))
```

The code fits the model, draws the two plots side by side, and then prints
the largest residual and the two counts.

The residual plot shows sixteen vertical stripes. The season
(`season`) takes only whole-number values, so only sixteen fitted values
exist. That is a feature of the predictor, not a violation. The vertical
spread is broadly similar across the stripes, so there is no strong
heteroskedasticity. The
Q-Q plot bends upwards at the right end: some pitches offered far more
equity than the fitted trend. The largest residual is about 83 percentage
points, from a founder who offered the whole company. As a benchmark, the
average offer is 13% of the company with a standard deviation of about 8
percentage points, so this residual is about 10 standard deviations of the
offers. So the normality
assumption probably does not hold. With $n = 1441$ this matters little for
tests and intervals, but you should look more closely at the extreme rows. Eighteen
standardised residuals lie beyond $\pm 3$, and 58 pitches have a Cook's
distance above $4/n$. These are about 1% and 4% of the 1,441 pitches.
:::

### Review questions from past lectures

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Using the Lecture 1 fitted equation
$\widehat{\text{agreed}} = -0.068 + 0.649 \times \text{claimed}$ (both in
\$ millions): a founder claimed a valuation of \$3 million and the deal
was agreed on air at \$1.5 million. Compute the fitted value and the residual.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

Fitted: $-0.068 + 0.649\times3 = 1.88$, about \$1.88 million. Residual:
$1.5 - 1.88 = -0.38$, about $-\$380{,}000$: the deal was agreed below the
model's fitted conditional mean, by about 20% of the fitted value.
:::

### Worked exam interpretation

**Exam-style question.** A regression
describes the monthly revenue of cafés by their opening hours per week. Its
residual-versus-fitted plot shows vertical spread increasing with the fitted
value. Name the pattern and the assumption it challenges. Then state one
assumption the plot cannot assess, and say what information would assess
it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check a model answer

The vertical spread of the residuals grows along the fitted values, like
a funnel. This is heteroskedasticity, so the pattern challenges
homoskedasticity. The plot cannot assess independence of observations. To
assess it, you need knowledge of the data collection, for example whether some cafés appear in several rows or
belong to the same chain.
:::

### Check the AI

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} You fitted the Lecture 1 regression of the agreed valuation on the claimed valuation. You asked an AI assistant: "My residuals look strange. What should I do?" It answered:

> "The agreed valuations are not normally distributed, so the regression is invalid. I removed the 25 outliers and now the model is fine."

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This task is the Verify
step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

Two errors. The outcome does not have to be normally distributed. The assumptions are about the errors and about how the data were produced. And you never remove unusual deals without saying so. Investigate them, report the fit with and without them, and say which one you use and why.
:::

### Make it yours

:::: {.utility-prompt}
<span class="label">Two sentences about your own venture</span>

Think of your own venture, or any business you know well. Think of a
regression you might one day run on its data (sales on advertising, orders
on price, sign-ups on campaign week). Write two sentences. First, name the
assumption from the table of assumptions in this lecture that you would worry about most for these
data. Second, describe one observation that could dominate the fit, and say
what you would do about it. Investigate it, check how much it changes the
results, and state openly what you do.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## See an example, then write your own

Take a student venture that sells boxes of prepared meals on campus. "For orders-on-price data I would worry most about zero conditional mean. I cut prices exactly in the weeks when demand is already weak. So weak demand affects both my price and my orders, and the price slope mixes the price cut with weak demand. One catering order of 200 meal boxes would dominate any fit. I would report the model with and without it as a sensitivity analysis, and investigate whether catering is a different business, not delete the row silently."
:::

You can discuss this task, and any other task in this chapter, with
Tilly for QM Intermediate, the course AI assistant: describe your venture's data
and ask it to argue which assumption is least plausible.
